intro: This guide takes your group through Amanda Smith: An Autobiography (For Teens) in twelve weeks, one chapter a week. It retells the life of Amanda Smith, born into slavery in Maryland in 1837, who became a washerwoman, an evangelist and a missionary preaching in England, India and West Africa. It is written for teenagers aged about 13 to 18 and suits a youth group, a homeschool or a small group.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand (5–10 minutes). Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you (10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Then close by praying, in your own words or inviting a volunteer to pray, about what the chapter raised (2–3 minutes). Each chapter ends with a “One thing to do” challenge, which is worth reading out before people leave.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself and glance at the activity; most weeks need only paper and pens. This is a true story with real pain in it: slavery and the selling of children, slave-catchers breaking into a home with violence, racism at school and in church, deep poverty, an unhappy marriage, and the deaths of Amanda’s children. Some in your group may have experienced racism, grief or hardship at home, so name the injustice plainly as the book does, let anyone affected speak only if they choose, and never make a young person explain their own experience for the group. Chapter 11 touches on differing Christian views about women preaching, so let the focus stay on Amanda’s calm, careful use of Scripture. Keep personal reflection private and be ready to talk one-to-one afterwards.

weeks.summary: Amanda Berry was born in Maryland in 1837 into slavery. Her father, Samuel Berry, worked late into the night making brooms and mats and labouring in other fields to buy first himself and then his family, and Amanda’s grandmother prayed for years for her grandchildren’s freedom. A young mistress, Celie, dying of typhoid, begged her family to let Samuel buy Amanda’s mother and the children, and Amanda later said she had been “bought twice, and set free twice.” The big idea: something can be legal and normal and still be wrong, and freedom that costs this much is worth taking seriously.

memory_verse.text: So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.

activity.title: Normal Is Not the Same as Right
steps: Point out from the chapter that slavery was legal and that respectable, church-going people took part in it.
Discuss: why do whole societies sometimes accept something wrong as normal?
In small groups, talk about how a Christian can test whether something is right rather than just normal or legal.
Discuss what Samuel Berry and Amanda’s grandmother did when the injustice was bigger than them.
Ask each person to write privately one freedom or gift they have never stopped to think about.

weeks.summary: Once free, the Berrys’ farm in Pennsylvania became a station on the Underground Railroad, and Amanda’s father walked miles at night to guide people escaping slavery. One night slave-catchers tricked their way in, beat her father and slashed at her mother, whose life was saved by the iron stove door, and the man they sought was caught. Another time her mother hid a man under the mattress with her small son on top, and the sheriff left laughing. The big idea: faith shows itself in brave, specific action for people in danger, even at real cost.

memory_verse.text: Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter.

activity.title: Do the Best You Can
steps: Read out Samuel Berry’s words: “Mother, I see four men coming; do the best you can.”
In small groups, list everyday situations where young people see someone excluded, targeted or pushed around.
For each, write one concrete, brave thing a person could do in the moment.
Share the best ideas and discuss what makes it hard to act straight away.
Ask each person to decide privately what they will do next time they see it happen.

weeks.summary: Amanda had only about three months of schooling in her whole childhood. She taught herself to read with letters cut from newspapers, nearly froze walking five miles to school one winter morning, and then often got only one lesson because the white children were taught first. The unfairness was real, yet it did not kill her hunger to learn. The big idea: a bad deal is not the same as a dead end.

memory_verse.text: The unfolding of your words gives light; it imparts understanding to the simple.

activity.title: Bad Deal or Dead End?
steps: Talk about how unfair Amanda’s schooling was, and why it matters not to smooth that over.
Draw two columns headed “What she was handed” and “What she did with it,” and fill them in together.
Ask each person to write privately one thing they have decided they “can’t” learn.
Have them write one small first step they could take on it this week, for fifteen minutes.

weeks.summary: As a casual believer in her teens, Amanda read a book written as a debate between a minister and an unbeliever, and the sceptic’s arguments stuck while the Christian’s faded. She became secretly afraid and miserable, and reading more of the same only tightened the snare. On a bridge she asked her aunt, “How do you know there is a God?” and her aunt refused to argue, gave her a piercing look and rebuked her, and the snare broke. The big idea: what we take in is not neutral, and a person who loves us can help free us from a trap of ideas.

memory_verse.text: See to it that no one takes you captive by philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elemental spirits of the world, and not according to Christ.

activity.title: What Is Shaping Me?
steps: Discuss Amanda’s point that she was intelligent and sincere and still got captured.
As a group, list the voices, channels and feeds that shape how teenagers see the world.
Discuss the chapter’s test: is this making me more truthful, or just more sure of things I never examined?
Ask each person to write privately one influence they want to look at honestly.
Encourage everyone to name, to themselves, one trusted older person they could talk to about their questions.

weeks.summary: Amanda wanted to become a Christian, but on her own terms, without a scene, and for months her strong will kept her stuck. One afternoon while ironing, tempted to give up, she heard “Pray once more,” answered “I WILL,” and went down into the cellar to pray until she was saved. When she stopped negotiating and said, “O, Lord, if Thou wilt help me I will believe Thee,” the burden rolled off and she came up full of joy. The big idea: seeking God with all our heart means dropping the conditions we try to set.

memory_verse.text: You will seek me and find me, when you seek me with all your heart.

activity.title: Dropping the Conditions
steps: Discuss the conditions Amanda set on coming to God, such as no scene and no going forward.
As a group, list conditions people today attach to taking God seriously, such as not looking weird or not giving something up.
Talk about why her strong will helped her in other ways but held her back here.
Ask each person to write privately the one condition they most want to drop, and keep it to themselves.

weeks.summary: Amanda’s younger sister Frances was born free, but in the chaos of the Civil War years she was sold in Maryland for forty dollars to a man for ten years. Amanda borrowed fifty dollars against her wages and travelled into a slave state alone, was refused even a drink of water, and found the man raging and demanding his forty dollars. With no one to protect Frances, Amanda paid the unjust price and spent years working off the debt. The big idea: love sometimes pays a price that is not fair, because the person matters more than the unfairness.

memory_verse.text: Give justice to the weak and the fatherless; maintain the right of the afflicted and the destitute.

activity.title: Fair or Loving?
steps: Ask the group to say honestly how this story makes them feel.
Discuss: Amanda had no duty to pay. Why did she pay anyway?
Talk about the difference between saying “that’s not fair, so I won’t” and choosing to put a person first.
Ask everyone to think privately of someone being treated unfairly who cannot fix it alone.
Challenge them to do one costly, helpful thing for that person this week.

weeks.summary: Amanda’s life held great loss: her first husband never returned from the Civil War, she buried children, only three of thirteen siblings lived to adulthood, and her second marriage was lonely and painful. Poor and exhausted, she sometimes washed clothes through the whole night. When Mother Jones found her crying at the washtub, she told her that what she needed was “enduring grace,” and Amanda saw she had been planning to get out of trials instead of asking God for grace to endure. The big idea: God’s grace is strong enough to carry us through what does not go away.

memory_verse.text: My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.

activity.title: Two Kinds of Prayer
steps: Read Mother Jones’s words about “enduring grace” aloud.
Write two prayers where all can see: “God, take this away” and “God, hold me up in this.”
Discuss when each prayer is right, and what Amanda learned about the second.
Ask each person to write privately a prayer for strength in one hard thing that may not vanish soon.
Talk about how the group could be a Mother Jones for someone who is grieving.

weeks.summary: Amanda went to Green Street Church in New York to hear John Inskip and found she was the only Black person there. As God met her, she wanted to shout for joy but held it in twice for fear the white congregation would put her out, until the words “you are all one in Christ Jesus” came to her with power. She stood and shouted “Glory to Jesus,” the preacher answered “Amen,” and afterwards the people she had feared “looked so small.” The big idea: in Christ our worth is not decided by race, class or anyone’s ranking.

memory_verse.text: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.

activity.title: The Mountain and the Molehill
steps: Discuss what Amanda had been taught all her life about where she ranked, and what finally broke that fear.
Read the memory verse and talk about what it does and does not mean.
Ask each person to write privately one place where they make themselves small.
Have them write one ordinary, honest thing they could do there next time.
Discuss as a group how a church or youth group can make sure no one feels they must shrink.

weeks.summary: Amanda became convinced God was calling her to preach in Salem, New Jersey, though she was a Black woman without ordination, salary or education, and knew no one there. She told only God her needs, including shoes, and days later an old man pressed five dollars into her hand. When the accusation came that people would say she was going alone to find a husband, she knelt and remembered God’s promise, “Did I not tell you that I would go with you?” and went in peace. The big idea: we can obey God’s leading even when it exposes us to what people might say.

memory_verse.text: Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak.

activity.title: God’s Guidance or the Crowd’s Opinion?
steps: List on paper every reason Amanda had to stay at home.
Discuss: which of these were real obstacles, and which were about what people might say?
In pairs, talk about how a person can tell God’s guidance apart from the crowd’s opinion.
Ask each person to write privately one right thing they have put off because of how it might look.
Challenge them to take the first step on it this week.

weeks.summary: Invited to England, Amanda first laughed at the idea of a washerwoman going and wrote a letter turning it down, because she was terrified of the sea. That night, in darkness she could not shake, she heard that she told others to trust God in the dark but would not do it herself, and she admitted it was true and repented. She crossed the ocean, and when proud passengers and churchgoers looked down on her, she held her head high as a child of God, “of the royal black.” The big idea: our actions should catch up with our words, and our worth comes from belonging to God.

memory_verse.text: And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

activity.title: Words and Nerve
steps: Discuss how Amanda had quietly exempted herself from her own message.
Ask each person to write privately one piece of advice they give others but find hard to follow themselves.
Next, have them write one way they could act on it this week.
As a group, discuss what it means that Amanda carried herself as royalty, and where that confidence came from.

weeks.summary: In India some Christians were offended that a woman was preaching and attacked her with letters and newspaper articles quoting Paul. Amanda, who usually never argued, read out from the same passage, “Let your men keep silence in the church,” to show that Paul was speaking about order in a chaotic meeting, and the attacks stopped. Earlier, watching a potter in Paris, she had prayed to be like clay that does not dictate, even in the furnace. The big idea: when people use Scripture or facts as weapons, answer calmly by knowing the truth well, and trust God with your reputation.

memory_verse.text: And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy.

activity.title: Out-Study, Don’t Out-Shout
steps: Talk about Amanda’s rule: “I never argue with anybody — just say my say and go on.”
As a group, list three ways people react when attacked: melting down, firing back, and Amanda’s way.
Discuss what it looks like to read a Bible verse in its context before using it.
Ask: what did the potter and the furnace teach Amanda about the opposition she faced?

weeks.summary: Amanda spent eight years in West Africa, where she learned she had been trusting in friends in America rather than in God, and help came once she trusted God alone. In Cape Palmas a boy named Bob often came to her gate, and his father, Jack, asked her to take him and teach him about God. Weak and without money, she was reluctant, but God answered, “You do what you can, and where you leave off, God will raise up somebody to do the rest,” so she took Bob to raise and educate. The big idea: we cannot fix everything, but we can do what we can and trust God with the rest.

memory_verse.text: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.

activity.title: Do What You Can
steps: As a group, list some problems in your school, town or world that feel too big to fix.
Pick one, and brainstorm small, real things a teenager could actually do about it.
Read the promise Amanda heard: “You do what you can, and where you leave off, God will raise up somebody to do the rest.”
Ask each person to choose privately one small thing to do this week.
Look back over Amanda’s whole life together and name the moment that stood out most.
